newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan keep eyes trained on peace talks.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan keep eyes trained on peace talks.

text.p: India and Pakistan, determined to keep peace hopes alive, have shaken off potentially destabilising reports about deployed missiles and a spy plane to keep their sights fixed on the next round of bilateral talks.
Last week the Washington Post reported India had deployed medium-range missiles near its western border with Pakistan.
The Prithvi missiles would for the first time give India the capability of targetting Pakistan's capital, Islamabad, with surface-to-surface ballistic weapons, diplomats said.

The report, denied by India, came less than a week after Pakistan said a sonic boom that rattled windows in Islamabad was caused by an Indian jet when it broke the sound barrier while flying out of Pakistani airspace on a spy mission.
New Delhi denied the aircraft was Indian and said the boom could have been produced by a plane outside of Pakistan's borders, perhaps within India.
In the past, such reports -- true or false -- could have cast a dangerous chill over relations between the arch-rivals, which have fought three wars since independence in 1947.
This time the reports drew predictable condemnation from Islamabad but authorities seemed unwilling to let them derail a fresh round of high-level talks set for later this month.
"We will not allow our process of political dialogue to be stampeded in any manner," Pakistan's high commissioner (ambassador) to India, Ashraf Jehangir Qazi, said on Saturday.

"Though such reports, prompted by some vested interests, unnecessarily vitiate the atmosphere, India has patience and capacity to take these in its stride. We are sincere in improving our ties with Pakistan," the Times of India quoted K. Raghunath, foreign secretary-designate, as saying on Saturday.
A diplomat in Delhi said: "Both sides are intently focused on getting the dialogue going. They are determined that this story should not stand in their way."
There was no independent confirmation of either report.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns refused to confirm whether India had moved Prithvi missiles to a prospective launch site in the northern state of Punjab.
But diplomats and analysts said India could not be expected to keep the Prithvi, which has been successfully tested in 250-km (150-mile) and 150-km (90-mile) variations, under wraps.
"This missile was tested in 1992," said former Indian foreign secretary J.N. Dixit. "If we develop a certain system, we don't keep it packaged up at home."

"It would not make a major difference if the missile was moved as it is not clear India has a working conventional warhead for it," a diplomat said. "The military significance of such a move is probably nil."

India and Pakistan say they have no nuclear arms but experts say either can assemble them swiftly. India held its only nuclear test in 1974. Pakistan says it has achieved nuclear capability without conducting any test.
Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral seemed determined not to allow the stir to derail talks between the two nations' foreign secretaries tentatively set to start on June 19.

Asked to comment on the reported Prithvi deployment, Gujral said: "It is more important to see the resolution passed by the U.S. Congress." He was referring to a resolution passed by the U.S. House of Representatives urging the Clinton administration to work closely with India to strengthen bilateral ties.

Sharif, in an interview to be aired on Indian television late on Sunday, had his sights on the long term. "We must get out of the hang-overs of past animosity," he said. "I want to come out of this frame of mind for a new beginning."

Dixit discounted the possibility, raised in the Indian press, that the U.S. government might have leaked the Prithvi report to put pressure on Delhi and Islamabad to place missile control on the top of their bilateral agenda.
